title: 13,000-Year-Old Bones Show Ancient Hunters Butchered Elephant-Like Beasts
summary:
Imagine an elephant with a longer, straighter trunk and a flatter head. That's a gomphothere (say it: GOM-fo-theer). Now imagine hunting one with nothing but stone tools. That's what some of the first people in South America did — 13,000 years ago.

Archaeologists digging along the shore of an ancient lake in central Chile found a huge pile of gomphothere bones mixed with stone tools. Many of the bones had clear cut marks on them. That means people butchered the animals right there.

The bones and tools date back 12,000 to 13,000 years. That's a big deal because it adds more evidence about when humans first reached the Americas. The oldest confirmed site in South America is Monte Verde, also in Chile, which is about 14,500 years old.

Scientists had already found bones of extinct horses and deer at the same lake, some with cut marks and signs of burning. So this wasn't a one-time stop. Ancient hunter-gatherers kept coming back to this lakeshore to hunt, cook, and eat.

Now the team will study the dirt and remains they collected. They want to pin down exactly when people lived there — and how they took down such massive animals.
why_it_matters: It shows that even with simple stone tools, people could take down animals far bigger than themselves — and it reminds us that our picture of history can change when new clues are dug up.

background_read: Chile is a long, thin country that stretches down the west coast of South America.
Monte Verde (an ancient campsite in Chile) is one of the oldest places where scientists have found signs of people living in the Americas.
For many years, most scientists thought the first people reached the Americas only about 13,000 years ago, so finds like this one make them rethink that story.
Article_Structure: WHO: Archaeologists digging along the shore of an ancient lake in central Chile
WHAT: They found a huge pile of gomphothere bones mixed with stone tools, and many bones had clear cut marks from butchering

perspectives.perspective: The archaeologists who found the site
perspectives.description: They believe the cut marks prove people hunted and butchered gomphotheres at the lake, adding a new clue about when humans reached South America.
Some researchers want stronger proof about the exact age of the bones before they agree people were hunting there that long ago.
